note:
'Why do you call Me good? No one is good except God alone' (Mark 10:18).

**Matthew's version of the saying does not survive the critical text that the Berean and the ASV follow.** There it reads 'Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is only One who is good', which removes the exchange about calling Jesus good altogether. Mark 10:18 reads the same in both, so the edge stands on Mark and Matthew is cited as the parallel it is in the KJV.

Recorded as implied because Matthew's verse says only 'Jesus replied' and never names the speaker; Mark names him and carries the pair.; 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' (Matt 27:46), spoken from the cross and quoting Psalm 22:1.; 'that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent' (John 17:3). **God-worded and Father-addressed** -- 'You' is the Father he is praying to -- which is why this verse is read both ways.; 'then the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all' (1Cor 15:28).; 'The head of Christ is God' (1Cor 11:3), in the same sentence as the head of every man and the head of the woman.; 'God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ' (Acts 2:36), spoken by Peter at Pentecost.; 'the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father' (Eph 1:17). **Names both in apposition**, which is why it counts on both sides.; 'I ascend to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God' (John 20:17). **The parallelism does the equating itself**, and the verse distinguishes him from both at once.

'The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father' (John 15:26) -- and in the same verse, 'whom I will send unto you from the Father'. **Both clauses are here**, and which of them governs is the question that divided East and West.

'how is it that Satan has filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit ... You have not lied to men, but to God' (Acts 5:3-4). **Consecutive verses, one act, both names**, which makes this the plainest statement of its kind in the corpus.

'the Father is greater than I' (John 14:28).; 'No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father' (Mark 13:32).; 'The Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it' (John 5:19).; 'I can do nothing by Myself ... I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me' (John 5:30).; 'The word that you hear is not My own, but it is from the Father who sent Me' (John 14:24).; 'Abba, Father, all things are possible to you ... However, not what I desire, but what you desire' (Mark 14:36), in Gethsemane.

'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). **Both clauses are in the one verse** -- with God, and God -- and the graph carries the verse rather than either half.; 'Thomas replied, My Lord and my God!' (John 20:28), spoken to Jesus and not corrected in the verse that follows.; 'they will call Him Immanuel (which means, God with us)' (Matt 1:23), quoting Isaiah 7:14. **The interpretation is the text's own**, supplied in the same sentence.; 'Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped' (Phil 2:6). The passage runs on to the servant's form and the exaltation, which is why it is read in opposite directions.

**The two translations pull opposite ways here.** The BSB reads 'did not consider equality with God something to be grasped'. The KJV suggests equality already held, so that claiming it was no theft; the BSB suggests equality not seized at. A reader leaning on this verse is leaning on a translation choice, and the graph says so rather than picking one.; 'Not only was He breaking the Sabbath, but He was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God' (John 5:18). **This is the narrator reporting how his hearers understood him**, not a claim in his own mouth, and the distinction is worth keeping.; 'The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation' (Col 1:15). Both halves are contested and both are here.; 'The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature' (Heb 1:3). The ASV reads 'the very image of his substance' -- person against substance, which is the vocabulary the creeds argue in, though the sense of the verse survives either way.; 'But about the Son He says: Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever' (Heb 1:8), quoting Psalm 45:6. **The Father addresses the Son as God**, and the words are an Old Testament citation, so the citation layer and this one meet in the same verse.; 'glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ' (Titus 2:13). Whether one person is named or two turns on the Greek article, which this graph does not hold.

'God the Father' in twelve verses -- 'Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' (Gal 1:3) -- and the two words stand together, not in apposition to anything else. Matthew 23:9 is the plainest: 'you have one Father, who is in heaven.'

**How consistently Paul does this is measurable, and it matters for reading the rest of him.** Every one of the thirteen letters carries the formula in chapter 1, eleven of them in the first three verses -- and then it essentially stops. Romans contains 144 verses naming God and exactly two joint formulas, 1:7 and 15:6: the greeting and the closing doxology, with the entire argument inside them. Nine of the thirteen use it once or twice in total.

So Paul specifies which God he means at the top of a letter and writes *God* thereafter. A reader who feels that his later, unqualified references are about the Father is responding to something real in the text. **The graph still does not re-point them**, because the inference only works if you already accept the identification this edge is careful not to assert. The pattern is recorded, at `grace_and_peace_from_god_our_father`, where it can be checked; the conclusion is left to the reader.
